strengths: Well-motivated problem identifying genuine gap between functional correctness and hardware efficiency optimization in RTL generation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across multiple benchmarks with strong empirical results (84.1% pass@5, significant PPA improvements)
Thorough ablation studies, sensitivity analysis across PDKs/tools, and scalability testing demonstrating robustness
Sound technical design of hierarchical rewards with gating mechanisms addressing learning-stage and scale mismatch
Extensive implementation details and reproducibility information in appendices
weaknesses: Poor fit for ACL venue: paper is fundamentally about hardware design optimization, not NLP/computational linguistics; LLM is primarily used as code generator rather than advancing NLP methods
Limited algorithmic novelty: CDPO is essentially PPO with standard curriculum learning and advantage-level aggregation; main novelty is problem-specific (EDA integration) rather than methodological
Data augmentation relies heavily on closed-source models (GPT-4o, DeepSeek-R1) with unclear validation of generated testbenches; this limits reproducibility
EDA toolchain integration lacks depth: reliability of PPA extraction unclear, computational costs during training not analyzed, sensitivity to reference design choice unexplored
Acknowledged weak performance on Control/Memory modules with only dataset scarcity explanation; no systematic failure analysis or mitigation strategy provided
Evaluation limitations: pass@k is indirect correctness measure, no human evaluation, pass@k on VerilogEval may overlap with training data
Technical underexploration: no ablation on key hyperparameters (β, curriculum schedule), no convergence analysis, minimal comparison to other multi-objective RL methods

strengths: Addresses a genuine practical problem: balancing functional correctness and hardware efficiency (PPA) optimization in Verilog generation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation with multiple benchmarks (VerilogEval, RTLLM v1.1/v2.0), extensive ablations, and sensitivity analysis across PDKs and synthesis tools

Well-engineered system with practical considerations: hierarchical reward gating mechanism reduces unnecessary expensive EDA invocations; runtime acceleration achieves 93.5% reduction in reward calculation time
Consistent empirical improvements over baselines (21.4% gain on RTLLM v1.1 pass@5, 20% EDAP reduction in worst case) across multiple base models
Thorough documentation: detailed implementation details, hyperparameters, prompt templates, and training procedures support reproducibility efforts
weaknesses: Fundamental venue mismatch for ACL: this is a hardware design automation paper, not a computational linguistics contribution. Core contribution is engineering an RL system for chip design, not advancing NLP/language technology or understanding

Limited algorithmic novelty: CDPO is PPO with curriculum annealing and weighting (standard techniques); hierarchical rewards and advantage-level aggregation are well-established RL approaches applied straightforwardly; builds primarily on existing VeRL framework

Reproducibility concerns: relies on proprietary models (GPT-5, DeepSeek-R1) for data generation that are not clearly defined or publicly available; no statistical significance testing despite extensive experiments; reference design quality and construction process unexplained

Experimental limitations: absolute performance remains modest (77% best pass rate means 23% failure rate); Table 11 shows failure cases (N/A entries) where ChipSeek generates non-functional code while baselines succeed, not adequately discussed; scalability degrades significantly on larger designs (53.3% pass@5 vs 84.1% on smaller designs)

Shallow analysis of why the method works: attribution of weak Control/Memory optimization to dataset scarcity is circular; no mechanistic understanding of learned representations or patterns; single barrel shifter case study is anecdotal; completely empirical with no theoretical justification

Generalization questions: evaluation limited to curated benchmark tasks normalized to specific references; most designs are <100 LoC; unclear how well methods transfer to novel out-of-distribution designs or production-scale hardware

Incomplete comparisons: no engagement with established multi-objective RL literature; no sample efficiency analysis; missing cost-benefit analysis of CDPO complexity versus simpler alternatives; limited discussion of computational cost (177.3s/step, 13×4 A100 GPU hours)

Methodological gaps: no significance testing or confidence intervals provided; dataset composition and diversity analysis missing (29K SFT + 8K RL samples); no empirical validation of circular dataset exclusion claims; PPA reward design (ref_m/gen_m) and weighting scheme choices unexplained

strengths: Well-motivated problem with clear practical gap: existing RTL generation methods achieve functional correctness but fail to optimize hardware efficiency (PPA metrics), clearly demonstrated in Figure 1

Comprehensive system design with principled technical approach: hierarchical reward structure grounded in EDA workflows (format→syntax→function→synthesis→PPA), computationally efficient gating mechanism, and preference-conditioned multi-objective optimization

Strong and consistent experimental results: achieves SOTA across multiple benchmarks (VerilogEval, RTLLM v1.1, v2.0) with 11.4% functional correctness improvement and 18-20% EDAP reduction; sustained across four base models

Rigorous experimental validation with thorough ablation studies: Tables 4, 5, 8 demonstrate contribution of each component; sensitivity analysis across PDKs, synthesis tools, and optimization targets (Appendix E); scalability shown on larger designs (~560 LoC)

Excellent reproducibility: detailed implementation specifications (Appendix B), algorithm pseudo-code, hyperparameter transparency, extensive appendices, and planned open-source release enable verification and follow-up work

Insightful case study demonstrating novel optimization: barrel shifter example shows model discovers synthesis-friendly behavioral descriptions rather than literal mux instantiation, yielding 13.3% area and 63.9% code reduction
Technically sound and well-presented: curriculum-guided advantage aggregation effectively handles scale mismatch between binary and continuous rewards; gating mechanism is computationally justified
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: CDPO combines three established techniques (advantage normalization, curriculum scheduling, preference weighting) without fundamental innovation in RL methodology; individual components well-studied

Questionable fit for ACL venue: this is fundamentally a CAD/EDA systems paper rather than a computational linguistics contribution; more appropriate for ICCAD, DAC, ASPLOS, or IEEE CAD; core contribution is domain-specific engineering rather than advancing LLM/NLP methodology

Incomplete failure mode analysis: acknowledges weakness on Control and Memory modules (Section 5) but only hypothesizes 'data scarcity' without systematic validation; some designs show 'N/A' (complete failures in Table 11) without analysis; no error categorization

Limited generalization evidence: sensitivity study (Appendix E) only varies PDK and synthesis tool, not specification formats; results only demonstrated up to ~560 LoC; unclear how method scales to 10K+ LoC industrial designs; all evaluation on standard benchmarks only

Significant computational requirements limit reproducibility: requires 13×4 A100 GPU hours for training (inaccessible to many); inference latency and memory footprint during deployment not discussed; even with 93.5% reward acceleration, absolute time still substantial

Data pipeline underspecified: 'online repositories' source vague; modest dataset sizes (29k SFT, 8.4k RL samples); filtering methodology to exclude benchmark cases not detailed; no analysis of potential data leakage or distribution bias

Preference mechanism lacks rigor: Equation 6 uses only binary preference vectors; no ablation on alternative weighting schemes (soft weights, non-uniform distributions); unclear how to elicit preferences in practice; trade-off discovery only implicit

Evaluation metrics have limitations: EDAP normalization against varying baselines; pass@k mixes functionally-correct designs with varying PPA; no confidence intervals or statistical significance testing; GPT-4/o1 comparison somewhat unfair (different resources available)
Limited ablations on design choices: no comparison of gating orders; curriculum annealing factor β not tuned/ablated; clipping bounds ε_low, ε_high not justified; why is w_func fixed in Eq. 6?

Tool and version dependencies not addressed: results depend on specific Yosys/OpenROAD versions; EDA tool improvements over time could obsolete results; reproducibility across tool versions not discussed
